🇺🇸 US proposes $5B fund to rebuild Gulf energy infrastructure
The Trump administration has proposed putting $5 billion into a new fund to repair Middle Eastern energy infrastructure damaged during the Iran war and reduce regional dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The US wants Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Iraq and Jordan to provide matching contributions, bringing the proposed Partnership for Allied Trust and Construction (PACT) to $10 billion.
The plan is still under discussion, and it remains unclear which countries will join. Some Gulf officials reportedly consider rebuilding before a peace deal with Tehran premature, warning that new infrastructure could again become vulnerable to missile and drone strikes.
💬 “This strategy has risk written all over it,” TRENDS US managing director Bilal Saab said.
The initiative follows extensive damage to pipelines, refineries and export terminals across the region during the seven-month conflict.

events.text:
🇴🇲 Oman emerges as Mideast gray cardinal with indispensable link to Ansar Allah
Donald Trump allegedly called off strikes against the Houthis at the eleventh hour on Sunday, even after military commanders had approved target lists and personnel were loading [munitions onto aircraft](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74837), The New York Times reports.
Previously, Trump rejected Saudi Arabia’s request to join its fight against the group. He later changed course — only to once again hold off on striking the Houthis.
Speaking to Fox News on September 20, Trump said the US was in constant communication with Ansar Allah, which had vowed not to attack US ships.
Oman arranged the communication channel between the US and the Houthis. Days after the group took control of Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and islands inside the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a US delegation met with the group’s representatives at the US Embassy in Muscat on September 13, according to Reuters.
On September 15, Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke by phone with his Omani counterpart, Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi, signaling Washington’s push to deepen ties with Oman – despite Trump’s earlier vow to “bomb the sh out of” Oman over its talks with Iran on [the Strait of Hormuz](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74667).
Last week, Saudi Arabia reportedly also reached out to Oman to relay a message to the Houthis. The proposal allegedly called for a two-week ceasefire and direct negotiations between Riyadh and the [Houthi leadership](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/74716), Lebanon’s Al Akhbar reported.
It remains unclear how the Houthi-Saudi communications played out, but Ansar Allah continues to advance against pro-Saudi forces, asserting control over Yemen’s Red Sea coast.
👍 [Substack](https://geopoliticsprime.substack.com/) | [Chat](https://t.me/+HLrnOk92f31mYzIy) |

events.text:
Turkey itching to relive Ottoman Empire’s crushing defeat to Yemeni tribesmen
“There may be military needs, particularly in certain technical areas, and we would have no problem meeting them,” Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan said in an interview after being asked whether the Houthis’ retaliatory strikes on Saudi Arabia were sufficient to activate the new [Mecca Pact alliance](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73259?single).
“We see very serious attacks against Saudi Arabia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty,” Fidan said, vowing that Turkey would “stand by our word” on its commitments to the alliance.
Besides military-technical support, Turkey is reportedly also mulling entry into a Saudi-led naval force in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Gulf of Aden – all areas where the Houthis have solidified their control over the past week.
 
Déjà vu?
 
Turkey’s military capabilities are nothing to sneeze at, with its forces deployed to Turkish Kurdistan, northern Iraq, Azerbaijan, Syria and Libya over the past decade to fight insurgencies or support Ankara-backed proxy forces, and its military hardware used in conflicts stretching from Karabakh to Ukraine.
But Yemen is another story. In nearly 400 years, Turkish Ottoman forces never managed to subdue the northern highland regions of Yemen – home of Zaydi Shia Islam and today, the Houthi movement. So fierce is Yemen’s historical reputation for thrashing its enemies that it became known as the “graveyard of Ottoman soldiers” due to the amount of troops lost trying to keep the empire’s grip on the region.
First occupied in 1538 as the Ottomans moved to secure Red Sea trade routes won from the Portuguese, Constantinople never succeeded in taming the Zaydi imams, who retreated to impregnable mountain fortresses, and waged nearly a century of warfare before totally expelling the Ottomans from Yemen in 1635.
When the Ottomans returned in the 1870s, the occupation proved even more disastrous, with their forces suffering up to tens of thousands of casualties each year at the hands of Zaydi tribesmen. In 1911, the empire essentially conceded defeat, exiting the region completely after 1918. The British, who had set up a protectorate in Aden in the 1800s, wisely decided not to try to conquer northern Yemen once the Ottomans left, leaving Yemen as the first modern Arab nation to achieve full, uncompromising independence in the 20th century.
